title: Cardiovascular I: Anatomy, Physiology and Heart Sounds
summary: How the heart pumps and what its sounds tell you.

lessons.title: Cardiac Anatomy and Coronary Circulation

levels.kid:
Your heart is a strong muscle about the size of your fist. It is a pump with four rooms. The two top rooms are called atria. They catch blood coming in. The two bottom rooms are called ventricles. They squeeze blood out.

The right side sends blood to your lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side sends that fresh blood to your whole body. Little doors called valves make sure blood only goes one way, like doors that only swing open forward.

The heart works hard, so it needs its own food too. Tiny pipes on its outside, called coronary arteries, bring it blood. If one of those pipes gets blocked, part of the heart muscle gets hurt. That is a heart attack.
levels.hs:
The heart has four chambers. Blood returning from the body enters the **right atrium** through the superior and inferior vena cava, passes the **tricuspid valve** into the **right ventricle**, and is pumped through the **pulmonary valve** into the pulmonary arteries and lungs. Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the **left atrium**, crosses the **mitral valve** into the **left ventricle**, and leaves through the **aortic valve** into the aorta.

The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps against the high pressure of the whole body, while the right ventricle only pumps to the low-pressure lungs.

The heart muscle (myocardium) is fed by the **coronary arteries**, which branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve:
- The **left main** splits into the **left anterior descending (LAD)**, which supplies the front of the heart and most of the septum, and the **circumflex**, which wraps around to the side.
- The **right coronary artery (RCA)** supplies the right ventricle, the bottom (inferior) wall, and usually the nodes that set the heartbeat.

Coronary arteries fill mostly during **diastole**, when the heart muscle relaxes and stops squeezing its own vessels.
levels.college:
The heart sits in the middle mediastinum inside the pericardium, rotated so the right ventricle forms most of the anterior surface and the left ventricle forms the apex and much of the left border. The atrioventricular (tricuspid, mitral) valves are tethered by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles, which contract during systole to prevent leaflet prolapse. The semilunar (pulmonary, aortic) valves have three cusps and no chordae.

The conduction system: the **sinoatrial (SA) node** in the right atrium near the superior vena cava sets the rate; impulses cross the atria to the **atrioventricular (AV) node** in the interatrial septum, which delays conduction so the atria finish emptying; then the **bundle of His**, right and left bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers activate the ventricles from endocardium to epicardium.

Coronary anatomy maps directly onto ECG territories:
- **LAD**: anterior wall and anterior two-thirds of the septum (leads V1–V4).
- **Circumflex**: lateral wall (I, aVL, V5–V6).
- **RCA**: right ventricle, inferior wall (II, III, aVF), and in most people the SA node and AV node.

**Dominance** is defined by which artery gives off the posterior descending artery (PDA): right-dominant in roughly 70–85% of people, left-dominant (circumflex) in a minority, codominant in the rest. Venous blood drains mainly via the great cardiac vein into the **coronary sinus**, which empties into the right atrium.

Because the left ventricular subendocardium is compressed during systole, left coronary flow occurs predominantly in diastole. Tachycardia shortens diastole, which is why fast heart rates can provoke ischemia in someone with narrowed coronaries.
levels.phd:
Coronary flow is governed by the pressure gradient across the bed and by resistance, most of which sits in the arterioles (<200 µm), not the epicardial conduit vessels. At rest, myocardium already extracts around 70–75% of delivered oxygen, the highest of any major organ, so increased demand must be met almost entirely by increasing flow rather than extraction. This is the core physiological vulnerability of the heart.

Flow is matched to demand through **metabolic autoregulation**: adenosine (from ATP breakdown), hypoxia, opening of ATP-sensitive potassium channels, nitric oxide, and CO2 dilate arterioles. Between roughly 60 and 140 mmHg of perfusion pressure, flow stays near constant. **Coronary flow reserve** is the ratio of maximal hyperemic flow to resting flow; an epicardial stenosis consumes this reserve by forcing downstream arterioles to dilate at rest. A lesion typically becomes flow-limiting at rest only when it is severe, whereas reserve is lost earlier, which explains exertional angina with normal resting function.

The transmural gradient matters: intramyocardial pressure is highest in the subendocardium during systole, so the subendocardium receives its flow almost entirely in diastole and is the first layer to become ischemic. Ischemia spreads as a wavefront from endocardium to epicardium, described classically by Reimer and Jennings in the 1970s, which is the physiological basis for the time-dependence of reperfusion benefit.

Collateral circulation varies widely between individuals and develops through arteriogenesis under chronic shear stress; well-developed collaterals can protect territory distal to a chronic total occlusion. The right ventricle, with lower wall stress, is perfused in both systole and diastole. Fractional flow reserve (FFR), the ratio of distal to aortic pressure at maximal hyperemia, operationalizes this physiology: it estimates the fraction of normal maximal flow a stenosed vessel still delivers.
levels.expert:
An attending reads coronary anatomy through the ECG and the patient's hemodynamics. ST elevation in II, III and aVF points to the inferior wall and usually the RCA; the next move is right-sided leads (V4R), because RV infarction makes the patient preload-dependent and prone to profound hypotension with nitrates. Inferior infarcts also bring bradycardia and AV block, since the RCA usually supplies the AV nodal artery; these blocks are often vagally mediated and transient.

Anterior ST elevation (V1–V4) implicates the LAD. A proximal LAD occlusion endangers a large area of myocardium and can cause cardiogenic shock; it may also be heralded by Wellens T waves (deep or biphasic T waves in V2–V3 in a pain-free patient), a warning not to send for exercise testing. Posterior infarction is easily missed: ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves should prompt posterior leads (V7–V9), as it may represent a circumflex or RCA occlusion that deserves emergent reperfusion.

Pitfalls:
- Treating a widow-maker pattern as stable because troponin is not yet up.
- Forgetting that left main disease can present as diffuse ST depression with ST elevation in aVR.
- Assuming dominance; the cath lab defines it, and it changes which territory an inferior infarct involves.

Surgeons think about targets: the left internal mammary artery to the LAD is the graft with the best long-term patency and is the foundation of bypass surgery. Interventional cardiologists think about lesion location, length, bifurcations, and calcification. In every case the shared question is the same: how much viable myocardium is at risk, and how fast can flow be restored?

keyPoints: Blood path: RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonary valve → lungs → LA → mitral → LV → aortic valve → aorta
The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps against systemic pressure
LAD feeds the anterior wall and septum; circumflex the lateral wall; RCA the RV, inferior wall and usually the SA and AV nodes
Dominance = which artery gives the posterior descending artery (usually the RCA)
Left coronary flow happens mostly in diastole, so tachycardia can provoke ischemia

examples.src: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF
examples.tr: Inferior wall infarct, most often from RCA occlusion; check right-sided leads for RV involvement.
Anterior wall infarct, usually the LAD.

test.q: Which chamber pumps blood into the aorta?
test.explain: The left ventricle ejects through the aortic valve into the aorta.

test.q: Which valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle?
test.explain: The mitral (bicuspid) valve guards the left AV junction; the tricuspid is on the right.

test.q: Why is the left ventricular wall thicker than the right?
choices: It pumps against higher systemic pressure
It receives blood from the body
test.explain: Wall thickness reflects workload: systemic pressure is far higher than pulmonary pressure.

test.q: The LAD mainly supplies:
choices: The inferior wall and the AV node
The anterior wall and most of the septum
The right ventricle and posterior wall
The lateral wall and the SA node
test.explain: The left anterior descending runs in the anterior interventricular groove supplying the anterior wall and anterior two-thirds of the septum.

test.q: In most people, the AV node is supplied by:
test.explain: Most people are right-dominant and the AV nodal artery comes from the RCA.

test.q: Coronary dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to the:
test.explain: Whichever artery supplies the PDA is dominant; usually the RCA.

test.q: When does most left coronary blood flow occur?
test.explain: Contracting myocardium squeezes intramural vessels, so left coronary flow is mostly diastolic.

test.q: The heart's pacemaker in normal rhythm is the:
test.explain: The SA node fires fastest and so sets the rate.

test.q: What do the chordae tendineae do?
choices: Conduct electrical signals from the AV node to the ventricles
Prevent AV valve leaflets from flipping back into the atria
Supply blood to the papillary muscles during diastole
Close the semilunar valves at the end of systole
test.explain: Chordae tether the AV valve leaflets to papillary muscles to prevent prolapse in systole.

test.q: Coronary venous blood drains into the right atrium through the coronary ___ (one word).
test.explain: The coronary sinus, in the posterior AV groove, empties into the right atrium.

test.q: ST elevation in II, III and aVF suggests an infarct of the ___ wall.
test.explain: Leads II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall, usually the RCA territory.

test.q: Which coronary artery (abbreviation) supplies the anterior wall?
test.explain: The left anterior descending artery supplies the anterior wall and septum.

test.q: The AV node ___ conduction so the atria can finish emptying before the ventricles contract.
test.explain: AV nodal delay allows atrial contraction to top up ventricular filling.

kidTest.q: How many rooms (chambers) does the heart have?
kidTest.explain: Two atria on top and two ventricles on the bottom.

kidTest.q: Where does the right side of the heart send blood?
kidTest.explain: The right side pumps blood to the lungs to get oxygen.

kidTest.q: What do heart valves do?
kidTest.explain: Valves are one-way doors.

kidTest.q: What feeds the heart muscle itself?
kidTest.explain: Coronary arteries on the heart's outside bring it blood.

kidTest.q: The bottom pumping rooms of the heart are called ___ .
kidTest.explain: Ventricles squeeze blood out; atria catch blood coming in.

kidTest.q: What happens if a coronary artery is blocked?
choices: Part of the heart muscle is hurt (heart attack)
The heart grows bigger right away
kidTest.explain: Blocked flow starves heart muscle of oxygen: a heart attack.

advancedTest.q: A patient with an inferior STEMI becomes very hypotensive after a nitrate. Most likely explanation?
choices: Left main coronary occlusion causing global ischemia
Right ventricular infarction making the patient preload-dependent
Aortic dissection, which the nitrate response excludes
Posterior wall rupture with immediate tamponade
advancedTest.explain: RV infarction (RCA) causes preload dependence; venodilators drop filling and output. Check V4R and give fluids rather than nitrates.

advancedTest.q: Why does exertional angina occur with a stenosis that causes no symptoms at rest?
choices: The plaque itself contracts with each heartbeat during exercise
Coronary flow reserve is exhausted before resting flow falls
Coronary flow occurs mainly in systole
advancedTest.explain: Arterioles downstream of the stenosis are already dilated, so flow cannot rise with demand; resting flow is preserved until stenosis is severe.

advancedTest.q: Why is the subendocardium most vulnerable to ischemia?
choices: It has no capillaries, so it relies on diffusion of oxygen from the blood in the chambers
It receives flow almost only in diastole because systolic intramural pressure is highest there
It is supplied only by the right coronary artery, which has the narrowest lumen
Its oxygen extraction is the lowest in the heart, so it wastes the oxygen delivered to it
advancedTest.explain: High systolic compression of the inner layer restricts its flow to diastole, so ischemia starts there and spreads outward.

advancedTest.q: Which conduit graft to the LAD has the best long-term patency in bypass surgery? (abbreviation)
advancedTest.explain: The left internal mammary (thoracic) artery to the LAD is the cornerstone graft of CABG.

lessons.title: The Cardiac Cycle

levels.kid:
Every heartbeat has two parts. First the heart relaxes and fills up with blood, like a sponge soaking up water. That part is called diastole. Then the heart squeezes hard and pushes the blood out. That part is called systole.

The top rooms give a little push first to help fill the bottom rooms. Then the bottom rooms give the big squeeze.

The valves open and close at just the right times, so blood never goes backward. When the valves snap shut, they make the sound a doctor hears with a stethoscope: lub-dub! Lub is the first set of doors closing, and dub is the second set. Your heart does this whole dance about once every second, all day and all night.
levels.hs:
The **cardiac cycle** is one complete heartbeat, split into **systole** (ventricles contract) and **diastole** (ventricles relax and fill).

In order, for the left side:
- **Filling (diastole):** the mitral valve is open; blood flows from the left atrium into the left ventricle. Late in diastole the atrium contracts (the "atrial kick") and adds a final top-up.
- **Isovolumetric contraction:** the ventricle starts squeezing. Pressure rises above atrial pressure, so the mitral valve closes (the first heart sound, S1). The aortic valve is still shut, so volume does not change.
- **Ejection:** when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the aortic valve opens and blood is ejected.
- **Isovolumetric relaxation:** the ventricle relaxes, pressure drops below aortic pressure, and the aortic valve closes (the second heart sound, S2). Both valves are shut.
- When pressure falls below atrial pressure, the mitral valve opens and filling starts again.

The volume left at the end of filling is the **end-diastolic volume**; what remains after ejection is the **end-systolic volume**. The difference is the **stroke volume**, and stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume is the **ejection fraction**, normally above about 50–55%.

At a normal resting rate, diastole lasts longer than systole. As the heart rate rises, diastole shortens much more than systole does.
levels.college:
The Wiggers diagram plots aortic, left ventricular and left atrial pressures, ventricular volume, the ECG and heart sounds against time. Its logic is that valves open and close passively according to pressure gradients.

- The **P wave** precedes atrial contraction, which produces the **a wave** of atrial (and jugular venous) pressure.
- The **QRS** precedes ventricular contraction. Mitral closure produces **S1**; the period until aortic opening is isovolumetric contraction, the phase of steepest pressure rise (dP/dt), an index of contractility.
- During ejection, aortic and ventricular pressures rise together then fall; the **T wave** corresponds to repolarization near the end of ejection.
- Aortic closure produces **S2** and the **dicrotic notch** (incisura) on the aortic trace, caused by brief backflow snapping the valve shut and elastic recoil of the aorta.
- Isovolumetric relaxation follows, then mitral opening and rapid passive filling, slow filling (diastasis), and atrial systole.

The atrial pressure trace has a, c and v waves: a = atrial contraction; c = bulging of the AV valve into the atrium during isovolumetric contraction; v = atrial filling against a closed AV valve, peaking just before it opens. The x descent follows atrial relaxation and the y descent follows AV valve opening.

The **pressure-volume loop** summarizes the cycle: bottom edge = filling, right edge = isovolumetric contraction at end-diastolic volume, top = ejection, left edge = isovolumetric relaxation. Its width is stroke volume and its area is stroke work. The right heart has the same sequence at lower pressures; pulmonary valve closure (P2) normally follows aortic closure (A2), splitting S2 with inspiration.
levels.phd:
The pressure-volume (PV) framework, developed by Suga and Sagawa, treats the ventricle as a time-varying elastance, E(t) = P(t)/[V(t) − V0]. Peak elastance occurs near end-systole, and the line through end-systolic PV points obtained at different loads, the **end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR)**, has a slope (Ees) that is relatively load-independent and serves as an index of contractility. The **end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship (EDPVR)** is exponential and describes passive chamber stiffness; its shift up and left defines impaired compliance.

Arterial elastance (Ea ≈ end-systolic pressure / stroke volume) represents afterload as seen by the ventricle. Ventricular-arterial coupling (Ea/Ees) determines efficiency: stroke work is maximal when the ratio approaches 1, while mechanical efficiency is optimal at lower ratios. Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction shows reduced Ees and increased Ea; heart failure with preserved ejection fraction often shows a steep EDPVR with high Ees and Ea, so small volume shifts produce large pressure swings.

Relaxation is an active, energy-requiring process: calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by SERCA, regulated by phospholamban, and detachment of crossbridges. The time constant of isovolumetric pressure decay (tau) quantifies it. Early diastolic filling is partly driven by ventricular suction from elastic recoil of titin and untwisting of the helical myocardial fibers; the normal ventricle fills mostly in early diastole, with the atrial contribution modest at rest but more important when relaxation is impaired or the rate is high.

The Frank-Starling mechanism has molecular roots in length-dependent activation: stretch increases myofilament calcium sensitivity, partly via reduced lattice spacing and titin strain. Doppler echocardiography reads these phases noninvasively: the E wave reflects early filling and the A wave atrial filling, and tissue Doppler (e′) indexes relaxation.
levels.expert:
Clinicians use the cardiac cycle at the bedside constantly, usually without naming it.

Timing a murmur depends on finding S1 and S2: palpate the carotid; the upstroke follows S1. A murmur between S1 and S2 is systolic, after S2 diastolic. Diastolic murmurs are always pathological; systolic murmurs may be innocent.

The jugular venous waveform is the right atrial pressure trace in real life:
- Absent a waves: atrial fibrillation.
- Cannon a waves: atrium contracting against a closed tricuspid valve, as in complete heart block or ventricular tachycardia (AV dissociation).
- Large v waves: tricuspid regurgitation.
- A steep y descent: constrictive pericarditis; a blunted y descent: tamponade.

Loss of the atrial kick matters most in a stiff ventricle. A patient with severe hypertensive hypertrophy or aortic stenosis who develops atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response may decompensate abruptly, because fast rates shorten diastole and the atrial contribution is gone at the same time. Rate control is therefore not cosmetic; it restores filling time.

On echo, the ejection fraction is a ratio, not a measure of output; a small, stiff ventricle can have a normal EF and a low stroke volume. Pitfalls include reading a 'normal EF' as 'normal heart' in someone short of breath, and interpreting E/A reversal without age context, since impaired relaxation is common in older adults.

In intensive care, the arterial line waveform shows the dicrotic notch; damping blurs it and underestimates systolic pressure. Pulse pressure variation with ventilation reflects how the cardiac cycle interacts with intrathoracic pressure and is used, with caveats, to judge fluid responsiveness.

keyPoints: Systole = ventricular contraction; diastole = relaxation and filling
S1 = mitral and tricuspid closure at the start of systole; S2 = aortic and pulmonary closure at its end
Isovolumetric phases: all valves closed, pressure changes without volume change
Stroke volume = EDV − ESV; ejection fraction = SV/EDV (normal above about 50–55%)
Faster heart rates shorten diastole most, reducing filling and coronary perfusion time

test.q: Systole refers to:
test.explain: Systole = the ventricles contract and eject.

test.q: S1 is caused by closure of the:
test.explain: S1 marks AV valve closure at the start of ventricular systole.

test.q: During isovolumetric contraction:
choices: Blood is ejected into the aorta
test.explain: Pressure rises with every valve shut, so volume cannot change.

test.q: The aortic valve opens when:
choices: Left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure
test.explain: Valves open passively when the upstream pressure is higher.

test.q: The 'atrial kick' happens:
test.explain: Atrial contraction tops up the ventricle at the end of diastole, just after the P wave.

test.q: As heart rate rises, which phase shortens the most?
test.explain: Diastole shortens disproportionately, limiting filling and coronary perfusion.

test.q: The dicrotic notch on the aortic pressure tracing marks:
test.explain: The incisura coincides with aortic valve closure (S2).

test.q: In a pressure-volume loop, the width of the loop equals:
test.explain: Width = EDV − ESV = stroke volume; area = stroke work.

test.q: The v wave of the atrial pressure trace reflects:
choices: Atrial filling against a closed AV valve
test.explain: The v wave builds as the atrium fills during ventricular systole.

test.q: Stroke volume = end-diastolic volume minus end-___ volume.
test.explain: SV = EDV − ESV.

test.q: EDV is 100 mL and ESV is 40 mL. What is the ejection fraction (as a percent)?
S2 is caused by closure of the aortic and ___ valves.
test.explain: A2 and P2 together make S2.

test.q: A normal ejection fraction is above about ___ percent.
test.explain: Most labs consider roughly 50–55% and above normal.

kidTest.q: What is the heart doing in diastole?
kidTest.explain: Diastole = relax and fill.

kidTest.q: What is the heart doing in systole?
kidTest.explain: Systole = the big squeeze.

kidTest.q: What makes the 'lub-dub' sound?
kidTest.explain: Closing valves make the heart sounds.

kidTest.q: Which rooms give the big squeeze?
kidTest.explain: Ventricles are the main pumps.

kidTest.q: The relaxing and filling part of a heartbeat is called ___ .
kidTest.explain: Diastole is the filling phase.

kidTest.q: About how often does your heart beat when you rest?
kidTest.explain: A resting heart beats roughly 60–100 times a minute.

advancedTest.q: Which index of contractility is relatively independent of preload and afterload?
choices: Slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (Ees)
Stroke volume measured by thermodilution catheter
Resting heart rate and its response to exercise
advancedTest.explain: ESPVR slope is relatively load-independent; EF depends heavily on afterload.

advancedTest.q: Cannon a waves in the jugular venous pulse suggest:
choices: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate
Tricuspid regurgitation with large systolic v waves
Cardiac tamponade with a blunted y descent
advancedTest.explain: The atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve when atria and ventricles beat independently.

advancedTest.q: A patient with severe LV hypertrophy develops rapid atrial fibrillation and pulmonary edema. Main mechanism?
choices: Increased afterload caused by the onset of fibrillation itself
Loss of atrial kick plus shortened diastole in a stiff ventricle
Mitral stenosis developing acutely from the arrhythmia
A shift in coronary dominance during the rapid rhythm
advancedTest.explain: Stiff ventricles depend on atrial contraction and filling time; AF with a fast rate removes both.

advancedTest.q: HFpEF on a PV-loop is classically characterized by:
choices: Reduced Ees with a large loop
advancedTest.explain: Stiff chambers show steep EDPVR: small volume increases raise pressure sharply.

lessons.title: Cardiac Output and Its Determinants

levels.kid:
Cardiac output is how much blood your heart pumps in one minute. Think of a water gun. How much water comes out depends on two things: how much water each squeeze pushes, and how many times you squeeze.

For your heart, each squeeze is a beat. The amount pushed out in one beat is the stroke volume. The number of beats in a minute is the heart rate. Multiply them and you get cardiac output.

When you run, your body needs more blood, so your heart beats faster and squeezes harder. When you rest, it slows down. If the heart gets weak, it cannot push enough blood, and a person feels tired and out of breath.
levels.hs:
**Cardiac output (CO)** is the volume of blood the heart pumps per minute:

**CO = heart rate × stroke volume.**

A resting adult pumps roughly 5 liters a minute, about the whole blood volume. During hard exercise a trained athlete can raise it several-fold.

Stroke volume depends on three things:
- **Preload:** how much the ventricle is stretched by filling before it contracts. More filling generally means a stronger contraction, the **Frank-Starling law**.
- **Afterload:** the resistance the ventricle must push against, mostly set by blood pressure in the aorta. Higher afterload lowers stroke volume.
- **Contractility:** the strength of the heart muscle independent of stretch. Adrenaline increases it; heart muscle damage decreases it.

Heart rate is set by the SA node and adjusted by the autonomic nervous system: sympathetic nerves speed it up, the vagus nerve slows it down.

Blood pressure is linked: **mean arterial pressure ≈ cardiac output × systemic vascular resistance.** That is why someone who bleeds heavily, losing preload, has a fast heart rate as the body tries to keep output and pressure up.
levels.college:
Cardiac output is regulated by intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms.

**Preload** is best defined as end-diastolic wall stress or sarcomere length, approximated clinically by end-diastolic volume or pressure. It rises with venous return (blood volume, venous tone, the skeletal muscle pump, lying flat) and falls with hemorrhage, dehydration, venodilation, or loss of atrial kick. The Frank-Starling curve plots stroke volume against preload: steep at low filling, flat at high filling. On the flat part, more fluid raises filling pressure and causes congestion without improving output.

**Afterload** is ventricular wall stress during ejection. By the Laplace relationship, wall stress ∝ (pressure × radius) / (2 × wall thickness). It rises with hypertension, aortic stenosis, and a dilated ventricle; concentric hypertrophy is an adaptation that normalizes wall stress.

**Contractility (inotropy)** increases with sympathetic β1 stimulation (cAMP → PKA → phosphorylation of L-type calcium channels and phospholamban), with higher heart rates (the Bowditch staircase effect), and with drugs that raise intracellular calcium. It falls with ischemia, acidosis, hypoxia, and myocardial loss.

The **Fick principle** measures output: CO = oxygen consumption / (arterial − venous oxygen content). A low mixed venous oxygen saturation means tissues are extracting more because delivery is low.

The **Guyton** model adds the venous side: venous return = (mean systemic filling pressure − right atrial pressure) / resistance to venous return. In steady state cardiac output equals venous return; the operating point is where the cardiac function curve meets the venous return curve. Increasing heart rate raises output only up to a point; above roughly 150–180 beats per minute in adults, shortened filling time reduces stroke volume enough to lower output.
levels.phd:
Intersecting the cardiac function curve with the venous return curve explains most bedside hemodynamics. Volume infusion and venoconstriction raise mean systemic filling pressure, shifting the venous return curve right; inotropes steepen the cardiac function curve; arteriolar dilation lowers resistance to venous return and rotates the venous return curve. In heart failure, sympathetic activation and renal sodium retention raise mean systemic filling pressure, preserving output at the cost of high atrial pressures and congestion.

At the cellular level, inotropy is a function of calcium transient amplitude and myofilament calcium sensitivity. Excitation-contraction coupling begins with L-type channel calcium entry triggering calcium-induced calcium release through ryanodine receptors (RyR2). Inotropes act on different steps: β-agonists and phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitors raise cAMP; digoxin inhibits the sodium-potassium ATPase, raising intracellular sodium and reducing calcium extrusion through the sodium-calcium exchanger; calcium sensitizers such as levosimendan bind troponin C. Myosin activators (omecamtiv mecarbil) prolong the force-generating state without increasing the calcium transient, a different energetic profile. Raising contractility increases oxygen consumption, which is a central concern in ischemic myocardium.

Afterload is properly a time-varying impedance, not a single resistance: input impedance spectra include a steady resistive component and a pulsatile component determined by arterial stiffness and wave reflection. Aortic stiffening with age speeds pulse-wave velocity so reflected waves return during systole rather than diastole, augmenting systolic pressure and LV load while reducing diastolic coronary perfusion pressure, a mechanism behind isolated systolic hypertension.

Myocardial oxygen demand is driven by wall stress, heart rate, and contractility; the pressure-volume area (the PV loop plus the potential energy region) correlates linearly with oxygen consumption. Treatment of angina and heart failure can be read as manipulating these determinants.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, an intensivist thinks of shock as a failure of one term in the output and pressure equations.

- **Hypovolemic shock** (low preload): flat neck veins, cool extremities, fast heart rate. Treatment restores volume.
- **Cardiogenic shock** (low contractility): cool, clammy, often congested lungs and raised jugular pressure; high filling pressures, low output, high systemic vascular resistance, low mixed venous saturation.
- **Distributive shock** (sepsis, anaphylaxis): low SVR, often warm peripheries early, high or normal output.
- **Obstructive shock** (tamponade, massive pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax): filling is mechanically blocked; the fix is relieving the obstruction.

Pitfalls:
- Treating every hypotension with fluid. The Frank-Starling curve is flat in a failing ventricle; more fluid produces pulmonary edema, not output. Assess fluid responsiveness (passive leg raise with a real-time output measure) before and after giving fluid.
- Trusting central venous pressure as a measure of volume status; it is a poor predictor of fluid responsiveness.
- Chasing a normal heart rate with rate-slowing drugs in someone whose tachycardia is compensating for a low stroke volume, which can precipitate collapse.
- Forgetting that beta-blocked patients may not mount a tachycardia when bleeding.

In aortic stenosis the afterload is fixed at the valve; vasodilators drop pressure without improving output, which is why they are used cautiously. In mitral regurgitation, lowering afterload increases forward flow. Inotropes buy time in cardiogenic shock but increase myocardial oxygen demand and arrhythmia risk; mechanical support and revascularization address the cause. The best cardiologists repeatedly ask which variable is broken and pick the intervention that targets that variable.

keyPoints: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume (about 5 L/min at rest)
Stroke volume depends on preload, afterload and contractility
Frank-Starling law: more stretch → stronger contraction, until the curve flattens
Mean arterial pressure ≈ cardiac output × systemic vascular resistance
Shock types map onto broken variables: preload (hypovolemic), contractility (cardiogenic), resistance (distributive), obstruction

examples.tr: Low preload → low stroke volume → compensatory tachycardia and vasoconstriction.

test.q: Cardiac output equals:
test.explain: CO = HR × SV.

test.q: Preload is best described as:
choices: Stretch of the ventricle before contraction
Heart rate measured over one minute
Strength and stiffness of the heart valves
test.explain: Preload = end-diastolic stretch, approximated by end-diastolic volume.

test.q: Which most directly increases afterload?
test.explain: Higher aortic pressure raises the load the LV must eject against.

test.q: The Frank-Starling law states that:
choices: Higher afterload raises stroke volume by stretching the walls
Greater ventricular filling increases stroke volume (to a limit)
Heart rate alone determines contractility and stroke volume
The heart valves open and close by active muscle contraction
test.explain: Increased stretch increases force of contraction within the physiological range.

test.q: Sympathetic stimulation of the heart:
test.explain: β1 stimulation is chronotropic and inotropic.

test.q: By Laplace, LV wall stress rises when:
test.explain: Wall stress ∝ pressure × radius / wall thickness; dilation raises stress.

test.q: Which shock type has LOW systemic vascular resistance?
test.explain: Distributive shock is defined by vasodilation (low SVR).

test.q: A low mixed venous oxygen saturation suggests:
choices: Low oxygen delivery relative to demand
test.explain: Tissues extract more oxygen when delivery (often output) is inadequate.

test.q: Above a very high heart rate, cardiac output falls because:
choices: Diastolic filling time becomes too short
test.explain: Short diastole reduces filling and therefore stroke volume.

test.q: Heart rate is 80 per minute and stroke volume is 60 mL. Cardiac output in liters per minute?
Mean arterial pressure ≈ cardiac output × systemic vascular ___ .
test.explain: MAP ≈ CO × SVR (ignoring central venous pressure).

test.q: What is the term for the intrinsic strength of contraction independent of preload and afterload?
test.explain: Contractility (inotropy) is the muscle's intrinsic force-generating capacity.

test.q: Fick principle: CO = oxygen consumption ÷ (arterial − ___ oxygen content).
test.explain: Output equals uptake divided by the arteriovenous oxygen difference.

kidTest.q: Cardiac output is how much blood the heart pumps in:
kidTest.explain: Output is measured per minute.

kidTest.q: What happens to your heart when you run?
choices: It stops for a little bit
kidTest.explain: Exercise raises heart rate and squeeze strength.

kidTest.q: The blood pushed out in one beat is the:
kidTest.explain: Stroke volume = blood per beat.

kidTest.q: How do you get cardiac output?
choices: Beats per minute times blood per beat
Add up your age in years
Count your breaths in a minute
kidTest.explain: Heart rate × stroke volume.

kidTest.q: The number of beats in a minute is called the heart ___ .
kidTest.explain: Heart rate = beats per minute.

kidTest.q: If the heart is weak, a person may feel:
kidTest.explain: Not enough blood reaches the body.

advancedTest.q: A hypotensive patient in cardiogenic shock has crackles and a raised JVP. What does further fluid most likely do?
choices: Raise cardiac output substantially by stretching fibers
Worsen pulmonary edema with little gain in output
Lower the filling pressures by diluting the blood
Fix the weakened contractility of the left ventricle
advancedTest.explain: On the flat part of the Starling curve, more volume raises pressures, not output.

choices: Stimulating β1-adrenergic receptors, raising cAMP and calcium entry through L-type channels
Inhibiting the Na+/K+-ATPase, reducing calcium extrusion via the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger
Blocking L-type calcium channels, which paradoxically increases calcium stored in the SR

advancedTest.q: Age-related aortic stiffening raises LV afterload mainly because:
choices: Blood becomes thicker with age, raising its viscosity
Faster pulse-wave velocity returns reflected waves during systole
Resting heart rate rises steadily with each decade
Preload falls as the ventricle becomes smaller

choices: A single central venous pressure value measured at the bedside
Passive leg raise with a real-time measure of stroke volume or output
Skin color, capillary refill and how warm the hands feel
The ejection fraction alone measured on a single echocardiogram

lessons.title: Heart Sounds and Murmurs

levels.kid:
When a doctor puts a stethoscope on your chest, they listen to your heart's music. A healthy heart says lub-dub, lub-dub. Lub is the first set of doors (valves) closing. Dub is the second set closing.

Sometimes the doctor hears an extra sound, like a whoosh. That whoosh is called a murmur. It happens when blood flows in a bumpy way, like water rushing through a pinched hose. Lots of kids have harmless murmurs that go away. Other murmurs mean a valve is too tight or leaky.

Doctors listen in a few different spots on the chest, because each valve is easiest to hear in its own place.
levels.hs:
**S1** ("lub") is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of systole. **S2** ("dub") is closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole.

S2 normally **splits** on breathing in: inspiration brings more blood to the right heart, so the pulmonary valve closes a little later than the aortic valve.

Extra sounds:
- **S3:** a low sound just after S2, from blood rushing into a ventricle. Normal in children and athletes; in older adults it suggests heart failure.
- **S4:** a sound just before S1, from the atrium pushing blood into a stiff ventricle. Suggests hypertrophy or ischemia.

A **murmur** is the sound of turbulent flow. Doctors describe it by timing (systolic or diastolic), location, loudness (graded 1–6), shape, and where it spreads.

Listening spots:
- Aortic: right upper sternal border.
- Pulmonary: left upper sternal border.
- Tricuspid: left lower sternal border.
- Mitral: apex (around the 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line).

Common examples: **aortic stenosis** causes a harsh systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border spreading to the neck; **mitral regurgitation** causes a blowing systolic murmur at the apex spreading to the armpit.
levels.college:
Systolic murmurs:
- **Aortic stenosis:** crescendo-decrescendo (ejection) murmur at the right second intercostal space radiating to the carotids; may have an ejection click in bicuspid valves; severe disease brings a soft or absent A2 and a slow-rising, weak carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus).
- **Mitral regurgitation:** holosystolic, blowing, at the apex radiating to the axilla.
- **Tricuspid regurgitation:** holosystolic at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration.
- **Ventricular septal defect:** harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border; smaller defects can be louder.
- **Mitral valve prolapse:** mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur.
- **Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy:** systolic murmur at the left sternal border that increases with less preload (standing, Valsalva).

Diastolic murmurs:
- **Aortic regurgitation:** early, decrescendo, high-pitched, best at the left sternal border with the patient sitting forward in expiration; wide pulse pressure.
- **Mitral stenosis:** opening snap after S2 followed by a low-pitched rumble at the apex, heard with the bell in the left lateral position.

Maneuvers separate lesions. Most murmurs (AS, MR) get softer with Valsalva or standing because less blood flows. HCM and MVP behave the opposite way: lower ventricular volume increases outflow obstruction or makes prolapse earlier. Handgrip raises afterload, increasing MR, AR and VSD murmurs and reducing the HCM murmur. Right-sided murmurs increase with inspiration (Carvallo's sign).

Splitting of S2: wide split with right bundle branch block or pulmonary stenosis; fixed split with an atrial septal defect; paradoxical split (on expiration) with left bundle branch block or severe aortic stenosis. Innocent murmurs are soft, systolic, with normal S2 and no symptoms.
levels.phd:
Murmurs arise when flow becomes turbulent, which depends on the Reynolds number: Re = (density × velocity × diameter) / viscosity. Turbulence increases with velocity (stenosis, high output) and lower viscosity (anemia), which is why fever, pregnancy, thyrotoxicosis, and anemia produce flow murmurs through normal valves. The pressure gradient across a stenosis follows the simplified Bernoulli equation used in Doppler echocardiography: ΔP ≈ 4v², with v the peak jet velocity in m/s. A peak aortic velocity of 4 m/s therefore implies a peak gradient near 64 mmHg, one of the criteria for severe aortic stenosis.

The intensity of a murmur correlates poorly with severity in several lesions. In aortic stenosis, falling output as the ventricle fails reduces flow and can make a critical stenosis softer, a pattern called low-flow, low-gradient stenosis, which needs stress testing to separate true severe stenosis from pseudo-severe disease. In mitral regurgitation, acute severe regurgitation into a non-dilated atrium equalizes pressures rapidly and produces a short, soft, early systolic murmur despite a catastrophic leak.

The timing of murmur peaks tracks gradients: as aortic stenosis worsens, the murmur peaks later in systole because ejection is prolonged. In mitral stenosis, a shorter interval between S2 and the opening snap means higher left atrial pressure and more severe stenosis.

S3 reflects abrupt deceleration of rapid early inflow in a ventricle with high filling pressure or volume, the hemodynamic basis for its prognostic weight in heart failure. S4 requires effective atrial contraction and is therefore absent in atrial fibrillation. Phonocardiography and modern AI-assisted digital stethoscopes quantify these acoustic features, but auscultatory accuracy among trainees varies widely, motivating structured teaching and echo correlation.
levels.expert:
An experienced clinician examines a murmur as part of a hemodynamic story rather than a sound to name.

First questions: is the patient symptomatic (exertional breathlessness, angina, syncope, palpitations), and are there signs of severity (pulse character, displaced apex, signs of failure)? Then time the murmur with the carotid pulse, locate it, and test it with maneuvers.

Red flags that mandate echocardiography: any diastolic murmur; a loud (grade 3 or more) or holosystolic murmur; symptoms; abnormal ECG; an abnormal S2; a new murmur in a febrile patient (endocarditis until proven otherwise); a new murmur after myocardial infarction.

Post-MI murmurs are emergencies: papillary muscle rupture (acute severe mitral regurgitation, flash pulmonary edema, often with inferior infarcts) and ventricular septal rupture (new harsh holosystolic murmur, often with a thrill, step-up in oxygen saturation in the right ventricle). Both typically occur within days and require urgent surgical or interventional repair.

In a young athlete with a systolic murmur, the screen for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the murmur that gets louder on standing from a squat or with Valsalva, plus family history of sudden death. This matters because HCM is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

Pitfalls:
- Calling a soft AS murmur mild in a patient with heart failure (low-flow AS).
- Missing aortic regurgitation because the patient was not sat forward in expiration.
- Assuming a holosystolic murmur in a feverish person who injects drugs is chronic, when it may be tricuspid endocarditis.

The stethoscope triages; the echocardiogram quantifies. A good examiner predicts the echo before reading it, then calibrates.

keyPoints: S1 = AV valve closure; S2 = semilunar valve closure; S2 splits on inspiration
S3 = early diastolic (normal in young, heart failure in older adults); S4 = late diastolic, stiff ventricle
Aortic stenosis: crescendo-decrescendo systolic at right upper sternal border → carotids
Mitral regurgitation: holosystolic blowing at the apex → axilla
Diastolic murmurs (AR, MS) are always pathological
HCM and MVP murmurs increase with Valsalva or standing; most others decrease

examples.src: Harsh systolic murmur at right 2nd intercostal space radiating to the neck, slow-rising pulse
Opening snap then low diastolic rumble at the apex

test.q: S1 is heard at the:
test.explain: AV valves close as ventricular systole begins.

test.q: Physiological splitting of S2 occurs during:
test.explain: Inspiration increases right-sided filling, delaying pulmonary valve closure.

test.q: An S4 suggests:
test.explain: S4 is atrial contraction into a non-compliant ventricle.

test.q: A harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids suggests:
test.explain: Classic ejection murmur of aortic stenosis.

test.q: A holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla is:
test.explain: Mitral regurgitation radiates toward the axilla.

test.q: An opening snap followed by a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex is:
test.explain: Classic mitral stenosis.

test.q: Which murmur gets LOUDER with Valsalva?
test.explain: Less preload worsens dynamic outflow obstruction in HCM.

test.q: Best position to hear aortic regurgitation:
choices: Lying flat on the right side
test.explain: Sitting forward brings the aortic root close to the chest wall.

test.q: A fixed split S2 suggests:
test.explain: With an ASD, right and left atrial pressures equalize so the split does not vary.

test.q: Which murmur is always pathological?
choices: A soft systolic flow murmur in a child
test.explain: Diastolic murmurs warrant echocardiography.

test.q: Turbulent blood flow heard with a stethoscope is called a ___ .
test.explain: Murmurs are sounds of turbulent flow.

test.q: Right-sided murmurs get louder on ___ .
test.explain: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart (Carvallo's sign).

test.q: A third heart sound, normal in young people, is called ___ .
test.explain: S3 comes just after S2 during rapid filling.

kidTest.q: What does a doctor use to listen to your heart?
kidTest.explain: A stethoscope carries heart sounds to the ears.

kidTest.q: What makes the 'lub' and 'dub'?
kidTest.explain: Each sound is a set of valves closing.

kidTest.q: A whooshing sound in the heart is called a:
kidTest.explain: Bumpy blood flow makes a murmur.

kidTest.q: Are some murmurs harmless?
choices: Yes, many kids have harmless ones
No, never, every murmur is bad
Only in grown-ups, not in kids
Only at night while you sleep
kidTest.explain: Innocent murmurs are common in children.

kidTest.q: A healthy heart sounds like lub-___ .
kidTest.explain: Lub-dub is the classic heart sound.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors listen in different spots?
choices: To tickle you on your chest
Each valve is easiest to hear in its own place
Because the heart moves around a lot
Just for fun, it doesn't matter
kidTest.explain: Different valves project to different areas.

advancedTest.q: Peak aortic jet velocity is 4 m/s. Using simplified Bernoulli, the peak gradient is about:
Three days after an inferior MI, a patient develops sudden pulmonary edema and a soft early systolic murmur. Most likely:
choices: Acute pericarditis with a three-part friction rub
Papillary muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation
Aortic stenosis with a harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur
An innocent flow murmur from fever and anemia
advancedTest.explain: Acute severe MR into a normal-size atrium can produce a soft, short murmur despite catastrophic regurgitation.

advancedTest.q: In mitral stenosis, a shorter S2–opening snap interval indicates:
choices: Milder stenosis with a lower left atrial pressure
Higher left atrial pressure and more severe stenosis
Coexisting aortic regurgitation with a wide pulse pressure
New atrial fibrillation with loss of the atrial kick
advancedTest.explain: Higher LA pressure opens the valve earlier after S2.

advancedTest.q: Paradoxical splitting of S2 is seen in:
advancedTest.explain: Delayed LV depolarization delays A2 past P2, so the split narrows on inspiration.
